problem: Many VLN and embodied-AI approaches rely on task-specific datasets, end-to-end learned policies or simulation-only setups that are hard to plug into standard robot navigation stacks. Turning a natural-language reference into a metric navigation goal that a conventional stack can execute is therefore not well served.
motivation: Non-expert users prefer commands like 'go to the mailbox' over coordinates or waypoints. VLMs can ground language in images, and RGB-D depth can lift the detection into metric space, so a lightweight, portable ROS 2 pipeline could connect language to Nav2.
key_idea: A remote VLM returns a bounding box for the object referenced in the user request, the box center plus a robust minimum-depth estimate is back-projected into a 3D point in the map frame, and that point is sent as a goal to Nav2.
insight: Language grounding can be separated from navigation: a frozen VLM gives a detection, classical pinhole geometry and TF give the goal, and Nav2 handles planning and obstacle avoidance. This lets the system run on different robots, with only topic and action interfaces reconfigured. Different prompt phrasings and viewpoints in Exp. 1 give nearly identical goals (errors 0.68-0.69 m), which suggests the perception is stable. The remaining error is dominated by the deliberate depth offset δ. There is no ablation and no baseline comparison, so the evidence is only qualitative and small-scale.
method: User Module: takes the natural-language request and returns the VLM's natural-language confirmation (e.g. 'Okay, I will go to the chair').
Communication Module: ROS 2 coordinator that abstracts the robot platform, acquires RGB and depth on request, calls the VLM and passes the goal to the Movement Module.

Semantic Perception (VLM grounding): sends the instruction and RGB image to a remote VLM server, which returns a bounding box (top-left, bottom-right) and a text reply; the box center is used as the target pixel.

Depth estimation: the depth is the minimum valid (nonzero, finite) value in a (2r+1)x(2r+1) window around the center pixel, to favor the object over the background; an object-dependent offset δ is subtracted (d' = d - δ) so the robot stops short of the target.
3D goal generation: back-projects the pixel with the pinhole model (X=(px-cx)d'/fx, Y=(py-cy)d'/fy, Z=d') and transforms it to the map frame with the ROS 2 TF transform mTc.
Movement Module: sends the map-frame goal to the Nav2 action server, which does global and local planning with costmaps from LiDAR and depth, and publishes cmd_vel; the module also monitors feedback.

setting.backbone: Unspecified remote VLM (frozen, accessed via server)
setting.observation: RGB-D camera (RealSense on Go2), robot localization/TF; LiDAR and depth for Nav2 costmaps
setting.action_space: Nav2 navigation goals in the map frame, executed as cmd_vel velocity commands
setting.simulator: Gazebo (TurtleBot3 Waffle) plus real world (Unitree Go2)
setting.privileged: none at test time (ground truth used only for evaluation); requires a localized robot and a map/TF frame

numbers.eval_set_note: 4 trials with different prompts and initial poses, single target (bus stop, δ=0.6 m)
numbers.extra: Simulation, goal-localization only, no navigation executed; ground-truth goal (18.0, 0.0)
numbers.evidence: Table 1 (Semantic perception evaluation, bus stop): Mean error 0.68; text 'average localization error of 0.68 m'
Table 2 (End-to-end navigation evaluation results) Mean row: 0.704, 26.0, 6.22

numbers.eval_set_note: 4 trials, 2 targets (microwave, chair), δ=0.5 m, Unitree Go2 with RealSense
numbers.extra: Localization only, no navigation; ground truth from manual measurement in the robot local frame
numbers.evidence: Table 3 (Real-world semantic perception evaluation results) Mean: 0.51

numbers_note: No standard benchmarks are used; all results are small custom trials (4-6 runs each) with no baselines. The VLM is never named, and no success rate is reported.
results: In simulation the bus-stop goal error averages 0.68 m over 4 prompt and pose variations. The full pipeline on a TurtleBot3 reaches targets with a mean error of 0.704 m, 26 s and 6.22 m traveled over 6 trials. On a real Unitree Go2 the mean localization error is 0.51 m over 4 trials. Nothing is compared against other methods.
limitations: The evaluation is tiny (4-6 trials per experiment) and there are no baselines, no success-rate metric and no ablations. The VLM is not named.

Only single-step, single-view detection is supported. There is no exploration or memory, so the target must be visible in the current image. The error is confounded with the hand-set per-object offset δ.
The real-world test evaluates perception only, not end-to-end navigation; multi-step tasks and dynamic environments are left as future work.
